qs.q: A 50-year-old man with insulin-treated diabetes and a history of cerebrovascular disease is being assessed via the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee score) prior to a high-risk vascular procedure. Which additional clinical feature contributes a point toward his index score?
qs.e: The Revised Cardiac Risk Index includes high-risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and a serum creatinine over 177 micromol/L. Obesity and hypertension are not independent variables in the Lee index.

exam: A 55‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden right‑sided weakness; CT is unavailable – what is your immediate management? — Assess airway, give aspirin if no bleed signs, correct glucose, arrange transfer for imaging.
How does hypertension cause both ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke? — Chronic pressure damages small vessels (lacunes) and leads to micro‑aneurysm rupture.
What features on exam help you distinguish a lacunar infarct from a cortical stroke? — Pure motor or sensory deficits without cortical signs (aphasia, visual field loss).
Why is clopidogrel preferred over aspirin in a patient with aspirin‑induced gastritis? — It provides antiplatelet effect with lower gastrointestinal irritation.
A patient on traditional herbal medicine develops a stroke; what should you consider? — Possible herbal anticoagulant effect or vasculitis; stop the herb and monitor coagulation.
Explain the rationale for blood pressure targets after an acute haemorrhagic stroke. — Lowering systolic <140 mmHg reduces expansion of the bleed while maintaining cerebral perfusion.
What red‑flag sign would prompt you to suspect a subarachnoid haemorrhage rather than an ischemic stroke? — Sudden thunderclap headache with neck stiffness.

How does HIV increase stroke risk, and what preventive steps are needed? — HIV‑associated vasculitis and opportunistic infections; ensure viral suppression, treat co‑infections, control traditional risk factors.
ai.title: Cerebrovascular Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Cerebrovascular disease (CVD) encompasses brain injury from disrupted blood flow, divided into ischemic and hemorrhagic types. In low‑resource settings, common causes include atherosclerosis, hypertension, HIV‑related vasculitis, and infections such as malaria or TB meningitis.

b: Ischemic: sudden focal deficit lasting >24 h with no bleed on CT/MRI.
Hemorrhagic: acute headache, vomiting, focal signs with bleed on CT.
sections.p: CVD is any acute or chronic brain injury caused by altered cerebral perfusion. Diagnosis rests on clinical syndrome (sudden focal deficit, altered consciousness) plus imaging when available.

b: NIHSS 0‑4: minor; 5‑15: moderate; >15: severe.
mRS 0‑2: independent; 3‑5: dependent; 6: death.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and by functional outcome using the Modified Rankin Scale (mRS).

b: Large‑artery atherosclerosis (hypertension, diabetes, smoking).
Cardio‑embolism (rheumatic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, HIV‑related cardiomyopathy).
Small‑vessel disease (lacunar infarcts from chronic hypertension).
Infections (TB meningitis, malaria, cerebral malaria, bacterial endocarditis).
Hemorrhage (hypertensive bleed, ruptured aneurysm, coagulopathy from malaria or herbal anticoagulants).
sections.p: Identify the aetiology to guide secondary prevention.

b: Sudden unilateral weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, visual field loss.
Severe headache, vomiting, decreased consciousness suggest haemorrhage.
Stepwise decline, gait disturbance may indicate vascular parkinsonism in chronic small‑vessel disease.
sections.p: Presentation varies with the vascular territory involved and whether the event is ischemic or hemorrhagic.
Select tests that answer the key clinical questions; adapt when imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Is the stroke ischemic or hemorrhagic? – Shows bleed; if negative, likely ischemic.
Is there large‑artery stenosis? – Detects >50 % stenosis needing possible endarterectomy.
Is a cardiac source present? – Identifies atrial fibrillation, valvular disease.

t.b: Are infection‑related causes present? – Detects malaria parasitaemia, HIV, anemia.
Is hypoglycaemia mimicking stroke? – Low glucose (<70 mg/dL) explains deficits.

b: Rapid neurological deterioration, new seizures, worsening headache – suspect expanding haemorrhage.
Airway compromise, aspiration, severe hypertension (>220/120 mmHg).
Complications: cerebral oedema, hemorrhagic transformation, deep vein thrombosis, post‑stroke depression.
sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent action and anticipate common sequelae.

b: Acute ischemic: give antiplatelet (aspirin) if no contraindication; consider thrombolysis if within 4.5 h and CT excludes bleed.
Acute hemorrhagic: control blood pressure (target <140 mmHg systolic), reverse coagulopathy, manage intracranial pressure.
Secondary prevention: aspirin or clopidogrel, statin, antihypertensives, treat HIV/TB/malaria, stop harmful herbal remedies.
Supportive: airway protection, physiotherapy, swallow assessment, treat fever and hyperglycaemia.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the brain, and prevent recurrence.

b: Blood pressure target <130/80 mmHg, LDL <70 mg/dL, smoking cessation.
Regular review of antiplatelet adherence, HIV viral load, malaria prophylaxis where endemic.
Community‑based rehab: gait training, speech therapy, education of caregivers.
sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on risk‑factor control and rehabilitation.

Hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, meningitis.
Brain tumour presenting with acute deficit.

Low platelet count from malaria may be misread as anticoagulant effect.
